Using the eSVD-DE embedding in the log fold change and its standard error: the embedding helps when the target is the effect at fixed cell state, and not otherwise

Kevin Z. Lin (drafted by Claude)

2026-11-11

Overview

This document is built from the design memo of the second loop (MEMO_claude.md), the record of its bank (BANK.md), the logs of its two runs, and the tables under csv/RUN_nov11/. Every number in its prose is read from those tables. It follows the sections of the autoresearch protocol’s run report, for two runs at once.

The question. The first loop kept donor_wls, a rule for the log fold change and its standard error that uses the fitted library of eSVD-DE and nothing of its embedding \(\widehat x_c^\top \widehat y_g\). Kevin asked for a second loop restricted to rules that use the embedding, on a bank in which cell-state differences give the low-rank term something to contribute. The question is whether such a rule exists, how much it gains, and what it estimates.

The document argues five things.

  1. Whether the embedding can help depends on the target. If the target is the log ratio of mean expression between the arms, cell-state differences included (the marginal effect), the embedding cannot improve the log fold change; if the target is the effect at fixed cell state (the direct effect), it can (Section 1.2).
  2. Scored against the marginal effect, the best rule found (embed_prior) ties donor_wls to the fourth digit, and its output does not change when the embedding is scrambled (Sections 3 and 5).
  3. Scored against the direct effect, the kept rule state_adjusted reaches -0.102 on the held-out split against 0.362 for the baseline and 0.345 for donor_wls, and the dev gain carried to test (Section 4).
  4. state_adjusted depends on the embedding: with the loadings and scores scrambled its log fold change moves by 0.64 to 1.44 standard errors where donors have states (Section 5).
  5. state_adjusted is wrong for the marginal effect wherever the arms differ in cell state, by construction, so the choice of target is the decision that precedes any choice of rule (Section 7).

How to read. A green box closes each results section with what that section changes. The blue box describes the simulated bank once, and a grey box opens each section that reuses it. The orange box in Section 7 is the procedure. A reader of the boxes alone gets the argument.

1 Definitions

1.1 Notation and the generator

A cohort has cells \(c\), genes \(g = 1, \dots, p\) and donors \(d = 1, \dots, n\) in two arms \(a \in \{0, 1\}\) of \(n_0\) controls and \(n_1\) cases. The bank’s counts follow

\[\log \mu_{cg} = \alpha_g + x_c^\top y_g + a\,\beta_g + \delta_{dg} + (\text{sex and age terms}), \qquad x_c = u_d + a\,s + e_c,\]

with \(A_{cg} \sim \text{Poisson}(\ell_c \lambda_{cg})\) and \(\lambda_{cg} \sim \text{Gamma}(\text{mean } \mu_{cg}, \text{rate } \gamma_g)\). The state \(x_c\) of a cell is its donor’s state \(u_d\), plus a shift \(s\) shared by every case cell, plus the cell’s own \(e_c\). The loadings \(y_g\) say how each gene responds to cell state. \(\delta_{dg}\) is the part of the donor’s effect that is idiosyncratic to the gene. Every donor term is centred so that its exponential has mean 1 within an arm.

eSVD-DE fits \(\widehat x_c\) (the scores, cells by \(k\)), \(\widehat y_g\) (the loadings, genes by \(k\)) and a coefficient \(\widehat z_{gk}\) per gene and covariate. Its reparameterization makes the scores orthogonal to every covariate, the arm included. \(\ell_{cg}\) below is the fitted library: the exponential of the fitted covariate terms other than the arm’s.

1.2 Two targets

The marginal effect \(\beta^{\text{marg}}_g = (\beta_g + s^\top y_g) / \ln 2\) is the log2 ratio of mean expression between the populations of case and control donors, at equal depth and covariates. A difference in cell state between the arms is part of it.

The direct effect \(\beta^{\text{dir}}_g = \beta_g / \ln 2\) is the effect at fixed cell state. A difference in cell state between the arms is excluded from it.

The two coincide unless the arms differ in cell state (\(s \ne 0\)). They differ in what the donors’ states do to an estimate. A cohort’s arms differ in mean donor state by \(s + (\bar u_1 - \bar u_0)\), the population shift plus the luck of which donors were sampled, and this moves the arm contrast of gene \(g\) by \(y_g^\top \{s + (\bar u_1 - \bar u_0)\}\).

  • For the direct effect all of that term is error. It lies along the loadings, so it can be estimated from the pattern of the arm contrast across genes and removed. This is where the embedding lowers the error of the log fold change.
  • For the marginal effect \(y_g^\top s\) is signal and \(y_g^\top (\bar u_1 - \bar u_0)\) is sampling error, and one cohort cannot tell them apart. An unbiased rule must keep the whole term and carry its sampling error in the SE. The embedding can then inform the SE and nothing else.

eSVD-DE’s own convention is the marginal one: the reparameterization moves the arm’s share of the embedding into the case-control coefficient. The memo fixed the marginal effect as the truth for that reason (its decision 1, made by Claude). Because the embedding cannot help the log fold change under that truth, the scorer was given a switch and a second run was scored against the direct effect.

1.3 The rules by name

Name in the tables Rule Uses the embedding Role
null_rescaled the pair that 1.2.0 stores (from donor averages of the posterior), shifted and rescaled by its empirical null through the posterior baseline of both runs
donor_wls the first loop’s kept rule: donor-level weighted regression of log pseudobulk ratios, moderated variance no reference, stored with the truth; not a candidate
deseq2 DESeq2 on donor pseudobulk counts no reference, stored with the truth
embed_prior donor_wls with the residual variance moderated toward a trend that also uses the donor variance the embedding predicts for the gene in the SE’s prior only kept by run A
state_adjusted Section 1.4 in the log fold change and the SE kept by run B

1.4 The kept rule of run B: state_adjusted

  1. Donor summary. With \(y_{dg}\) the donor’s summed counts and \(L_{dg} = \sum_{c \in d} \ell_{cg}\), \(l_{dg} = \log\{(y_{dg} + 1/2) / L_{dg}\}\).
  2. Design. \(D\) is the \(n \times q\) donor-level matrix of the intercept, the arm, and every covariate constant within donors.
  3. Embedding offset. The donor’s embedding offset is \[e_{dg} = \log\frac{\sum_{c \in d} \ell_{cg} \exp(\widehat x_c^\top \widehat y_g)}{L_{dg}},\] \(e^{r}_{dg}\) is its least-squares residual on \(D\), and \(b = \sum_{d,g} e^{r}_{dg}\, l^{r}_{dg} / \sum_{d,g} (e^{r}_{dg})^2\), with \(l^{r}\) the residual of \(l\) on \(D\), is one coefficient per cohort.
  4. Donor-level regression. \(l_{dg} - b\, e^{r}_{dg}\) is regressed on \(D\) as in donor_wls (donor offsets, precision weights from \(\tau^2 + \phi / \mu_{dg}\), weighted least squares). This gives the arm coefficient \(\widehat\theta_g\), its variance factor \(a_g\), and the residual variance \(S_g\) on \(\nu = n - q\) degrees of freedom, moderated across genes to \(\widetilde S_g\). Because \(e^{r}\) is orthogonal to the arm, \(\widehat\theta_g\) is the arm contrast of \(l\) itself; subtracting \(b\, e^{r}\) only takes the donor-to-donor variation along the embedding out of \(S_g\). Write \(v_g = a_g \widetilde S_g\).
  5. Loadings regression. With \(m_g = (1,\; \widehat y_g,\; \{\widehat y_{gj} \widehat y_{gj'}\}_{j \le j'})\), \(\widehat\theta_g\) is regressed on \(m_g\) over the genes with weights \(1 / v_g\), in two passes, the second without the genes whose residual exceeded \(3 \sqrt{v_g}\) in the first. The fitted coefficients are an intercept \(c_0\), a vector \(\widehat d\) on the loadings and a symmetric matrix \(\widehat Q\) on their products.
  6. The pair before calibration. \[\widehat\beta^{\,0}_g = \frac{\widehat\theta_g - \widehat y_g^\top \widehat d - \widehat y_g^\top \widehat Q\, \widehat y_g}{\ln 2}, \qquad s^{0}_g = \frac{\sqrt{v_g + h_g}}{\ln 2},\] with \(h_g\) the leverage of gene \(g\)’s loading terms in that regression.
  7. Calibration. With \((\delta_0, \sigma_0)\) the mean and SD of the empirical null fitted by eSVD2::multtest() to \(\widehat\beta^{\,0}_g / s^{0}_g\) and \(f = \min\{\max(\sigma_0, 1),\; \sqrt{\nu / \max(\nu - k, 1)}\}\), the rule reports \[\widehat\beta_g = \widehat\beta^{\,0}_g - \delta_0 \cdot \text{median}_g\, s^{0}_g, \qquad s_g = f\, s^{0}_g .\]

Where the embedding enters, and why.

  • Step 5, the linear term (the log fold change). The arms’ difference in mean donor state moves \(\widehat\theta_g\) by \(y_g^\top d\). The fit holds the scores orthogonal to the arm, so that term is not in the scores; it is in the arm contrast, along the loadings, and \(\widehat d\) is five numbers estimated from 600 genes.
  • Step 5, the quadratic term (the log fold change). \(\widehat\theta_g\) is a contrast of mean log expression, which differs from the log ratio of mean expression by half the difference of the arms’ donor variances on the log scale. The part of that difference that comes from donor states is \(y_g^\top (\Sigma_1 - \Sigma_0)\, y_g / 2\), a quadratic form in the loadings, and \(\widehat Q\) estimates it.
  • Step 3 (the SE). The states’ donor-to-donor variation no longer moves \(\widehat\beta^{\,0}_g\) once step 5 has removed its arm contrast, so it must leave the variance too, and \(b\, e^{r}\) takes it out of \(S_g\).
  • Step 7 (the SE). The offset was fitted to the same counts and absorbs part of the idiosyncratic donor noise within arms, while the arm contrast of that noise went to the case-control coefficient and stays in \(\widehat\theta_g\). \(S_g\) therefore understates, by a factor that the empirical null measures and that the offset’s \(k\) free directions among \(\nu\) bound.
# `state_adjusted`: the reporting rule kept by run B (`autoresearch_lfcse2/
# nov11-direct`) of the second autoresearch loop: a log2 fold change at
# fixed cell state, and its standard error, from one fitted eSVD-DE cohort.
# Drafted by Claude for Kevin Z. Lin, 2026-11-11.
#
# Mirrors commit 1cfd07b of `autoresearch_lfcse2/report_rule_claude.R` (the
# code is identical; only this header differs).
# Score: Gaussian negative log-likelihood of the true log2 fold change at
# fixed cell state (ESVD2_TRUTH=direct), nats per gene, lower is better, on
# the bank `lfcse-bank-2`.
#              baseline `null_rescaled`   `donor_wls`   this rule
#   dev            0.3576                   0.3569        -0.0943
#   test           0.3620                   0.3447        -0.1020
#
# Use: `res_df <- report_lfc_se(view)`, where `view` is a list holding what
# a user has after `eSVD()` with `bool_diet = FALSE`. The rule reads
#   view$dat               counts, cells x genes, with gene names as colnames
#   view$library_mat       fitted library size per cell and gene
#   view$covariates        the design matrix of the fit, cells x covariates
#   view$individual_vec    donor of each cell
#   view$case_control_vec  arm of each cell, 1 for cases and 0 for controls
#   view$x_mat, view$y_mat the fitted embedding (cells x k, genes x k)
# and returns a data frame with one row per gene and columns `gene`,
# `log2fc`, `se`. It needs the packages `stats` and `eSVD2` (for
# `eSVD2::multtest()`, which calls `locfdr`).
#
# The rule estimates the case-control effect at fixed cell state: the part
# of the arm contrast that runs along the embedding's loadings is treated
# as a difference in cell state between the arms' donors and removed.
#
# Each donor is summarized, gene by gene, by l = log((summed counts + 1/2)
# / summed fitted library), and by its embedding offset e = log of the
# library-weighted mean over its cells of exp(x' y). Let e_r be the
# residual of e on the donor-level design D (intercept, arm, covariates
# constant within donors) and b the one coefficient per cohort of the
# least-squares regression of the residuals of l on e_r over all donors
# and genes. Then l - b e_r is regressed on D with precision weights, which
# gives the arm coefficient theta_g (that of l, since e_r is orthogonal to
# the arm), its variance factor a and a residual variance S free of the
# donor-to-donor variation along the embedding.
#
# The fit's reparameterization makes the embedding orthogonal to the arm,
# so the arms' difference in cell state sits in theta as a term y_g' d.
# The vector d is estimated by weighted least squares of theta_g on the
# loadings y_g over the genes (with an intercept; weights 1 / (a S~); a
# second pass leaves out the genes whose residual is beyond 3 SE, which
# carry an effect of their own). The regression also holds the products
# y_gj y_gk of the loadings: theta is a contrast of mean log expression,
# which differs from the log ratio of mean expression by half the
# difference of the arms' donor variances, and the embedding's part of
# that difference is y_g' (Sigma_1 - Sigma_0) y_g / 2, a quadratic form in
# the loadings. Then
#   lfc_g = (theta_g - y_g' d) / ln 2,
#   se_g^2 = (a S~ + y_g' Cov(d) y_g) / (ln 2)^2,
# with S~ the moderated S. The embedding offset was fitted to the same
# counts, so S understates what is left in theta; the SE is rescaled by the
# SD of the empirical null fitted to lfc / se, held between 1 (the offset
# cannot make S too large) and sqrt(df / (df - k)) (the offset has k free
# directions among the df = n - rank(D) residual ones, so it cannot have
# absorbed more than that share). The logFC is shifted by the null's mean
# times the median SE.

# Inverse of the trigamma function by Newton's method on its reciprocal
# (Smyth 2004, appendix); the start 0.5 + 1 / x is exact in both limits.
.trigamma_inverse <- function(x_val){
  y_val <- 0.5 + 1 / x_val
  for(iter in seq_len(50)){
    tri <- trigamma(y_val)
    step <- tri * (1 - tri / x_val) / psigamma(y_val, deriv = 2)
    y_val <- y_val + step
    # Relative step below single precision: converged.
    if(-step / y_val < 1e-8) break
  }
  y_val
}

# Moderate per-gene variances `var_vec`, each with `df` degrees of
# freedom, toward their trend in `covariate_vec` (Smyth 2004): the trend is
# a smoothing spline of the log variance, the excess of the residual
# variance over trigamma(df / 2) gives the prior degrees of freedom d0, and
# the moderated variance is (d0 * s0^2 + df * var) / (d0 + df).
.moderate_variance <- function(var_vec, df, covariate_vec){
  idx <- which(is.finite(var_vec) & var_vec > 0 & is.finite(covariate_vec))
  log_vec <- log(var_vec[idx])
  spline_fit <- stats::smooth.spline(x = covariate_vec[idx], y = log_vec)
  trend_vec <- stats::predict(spline_fit, x = covariate_vec)$y
  excess <- mean((log_vec - trend_vec[idx])^2) - trigamma(df / 2)
  if(excess <= 0){
    # No spread beyond sampling noise: every gene takes the trend.
    return(exp(trend_vec - digamma(df / 2) + log(df / 2)))
  }
  prior_df <- 2 * .trigamma_inverse(excess)
  prior_vec <- exp(trend_vec - digamma(df / 2) + log(df / 2) +
                     digamma(prior_df / 2) - log(prior_df / 2))
  (prior_df * prior_vec + df * var_vec) / (prior_df + df)
}

# The donor-level design: intercept, arm, and every column of `covariates`
# that is constant within donors (sex, age).
.donor_design <- function(covariates, individual_vec, arm_vec, donor_vec){
  individual_chr <- as.character(individual_vec)
  first_idx <- match(donor_vec, individual_chr)
  bool_donor_level <- apply(covariates, 2, function(col_vec){
    all(col_vec == col_vec[first_idx][match(individual_chr, donor_vec)])
  })
  design_mat <- cbind(1, arm_vec,
                      covariates[first_idx, bool_donor_level, drop = FALSE])
  qr_res <- qr(design_mat)
  # Columns 1 and 2 (intercept, arm) are pivoted first, so the constant
  # and arm columns of `covariates` itself drop out as redundant.
  design_mat[, qr_res$pivot[seq_len(qr_res$rank)], drop = FALSE]
}

.least_squares_fit <- function(design_mat, response_mat){
  design_mat %*% solve(crossprod(design_mat),
                       crossprod(design_mat, response_mat))
}

# Weighted least squares of each column of `log_mat` on `design_mat`, with
# precision weights from the two-part variance tau^2 + phi / (expected
# count) fitted over all donors and genes. Returns the arm coefficient
# (natural log), its variance factor, the residual variance on
# n - rank(design) degrees of freedom, the mean fitted value, and the
# weights.
.donor_regression <- function(log_mat, library_sum_mat, design_mat){
  fit_mat <- .least_squares_fit(design_mat, log_mat)
  # A donor's offset common to all genes: the median over genes of its
  # residuals, removed before the variance is estimated.
  log_mat <- log_mat - apply(log_mat - fit_mat, 1, stats::median)
  fit_mat <- .least_squares_fit(design_mat, log_mat)
  residual_df <- nrow(design_mat) - ncol(design_mat)
  inverse_count_vec <- as.numeric(exp(-(fit_mat + log(library_sum_mat))))
  squared_vec <- as.numeric((log_mat - fit_mat)^2) *
    nrow(design_mat) / residual_df
  slope <- stats::cov(squared_vec, inverse_count_vec) /
    stats::var(inverse_count_vec)
  # Neither part of a variance can be negative.
  variance_coef <- pmax(c(mean(squared_vec) -
                            slope * mean(inverse_count_vec), slope), 0)
  weight_mat <- matrix(1 / (variance_coef[1] +
                              variance_coef[2] * inverse_count_vec),
                       nrow = nrow(fit_mat))
  num_genes <- ncol(log_mat)
  coef_arm_vec <- numeric(num_genes)
  arm_var_vec <- numeric(num_genes)
  residual_var <- numeric(num_genes)
  for(j in seq_len(num_genes)){
    weighted_design <- design_mat * weight_mat[, j]
    gram_inv_mat <- solve(crossprod(design_mat, weighted_design))
    coef_vec <- gram_inv_mat %*% crossprod(weighted_design, log_mat[, j])
    coef_arm_vec[j] <- coef_vec[2]
    arm_var_vec[j] <- gram_inv_mat[2, 2]
    residual_var[j] <- sum(weight_mat[, j] *
                             (log_mat[, j] - design_mat %*% coef_vec)^2) /
      residual_df
  }
  list(arm_var_vec = arm_var_vec,
       coef_arm_vec = coef_arm_vec,
       level_vec = colMeans(fit_mat),
       residual_df = residual_df,
       residual_var = residual_var,
       weight_mat = weight_mat)
}

report_lfc_se <- function(view){
  individual_chr <- as.character(view$individual_vec)
  library_sum_mat <- rowsum(view$library_mat, group = individual_chr)
  donor_vec <- rownames(library_sum_mat)
  count_mat <- rowsum(view$dat, group = individual_chr)
  # Half a count keeps the logarithm of a donor with no count finite (the
  # continuity correction of a Poisson count).
  raw_mat <- log((count_mat + 0.5) / library_sum_mat)
  # The embedding offset of each donor and gene.
  embedding_mat <- exp(tcrossprod(view$x_mat, view$y_mat))
  offset_mat <- log(rowsum(view$library_mat * embedding_mat,
                           group = individual_chr) / library_sum_mat)
  arm_vec <- view$case_control_vec[match(donor_vec, individual_chr)]
  design_mat <- .donor_design(covariates = view$covariates,
                              individual_vec = view$individual_vec,
                              arm_vec = arm_vec, donor_vec = donor_vec)
  # The offset's residual on the design, and its one coefficient.
  offset_res_mat <- offset_mat - .least_squares_fit(design_mat, offset_mat)
  raw_res_mat <- raw_mat - .least_squares_fit(design_mat, raw_mat)
  offset_coef <- sum(offset_res_mat * raw_res_mat) / sum(offset_res_mat^2)

  res <- .donor_regression(log_mat = raw_mat - offset_coef * offset_res_mat,
                           library_sum_mat = library_sum_mat,
                           design_mat = design_mat)
  noise_var_vec <- res$arm_var_vec *
    .moderate_variance(var_vec = res$residual_var, df = res$residual_df,
                       covariate_vec = res$level_vec)
  # The arms' difference in cell state: the arm coefficients regressed on
  # the loadings over the genes, each gene weighted by its precision.
  # The loadings and their pairwise products (squares included).
  num_factors <- ncol(view$y_mat)
  pair_idx_mat <- which(upper.tri(diag(num_factors), diag = TRUE),
                        arr.ind = TRUE)
  product_mat <- view$y_mat[, pair_idx_mat[, 1], drop = FALSE] *
    view$y_mat[, pair_idx_mat[, 2], drop = FALSE]
  loading_mat <- cbind(1, view$y_mat, product_mat)
  bool_use <- rep(TRUE, nrow(loading_mat))
  # Two passes: the second without the genes that the first leaves beyond
  # 3 SE (a normal residual is beyond 3 SE once in 370 genes).
  for(pass in seq_len(2)){
    weighted_mat <- loading_mat[bool_use, , drop = FALSE] /
      noise_var_vec[bool_use]
    gram_inv_mat <- solve(crossprod(loading_mat[bool_use, , drop = FALSE],
                                    weighted_mat))
    state_coef_vec <- gram_inv_mat %*%
      crossprod(weighted_mat, res$coef_arm_vec[bool_use])
    fitted_vec <- as.numeric(loading_mat %*% state_coef_vec)
    bool_use <- abs(res$coef_arm_vec - fitted_vec) <= 3 * sqrt(noise_var_vec)
  }
  # The intercept stays in the logFC; the empirical null centres it below.
  state_part_vec <- fitted_vec - state_coef_vec[1]
  lfc_vec <- (res$coef_arm_vec - state_part_vec) / log(2)
  # The variance of the removed part: the loadings' leverage under the
  # weights.
  state_var_vec <- rowSums((loading_mat[, -1, drop = FALSE] %*%
                              gram_inv_mat[-1, -1, drop = FALSE]) *
                             loading_mat[, -1, drop = FALSE])
  se_vec <- sqrt(noise_var_vec + state_var_vec) / log(2)

  z_vec <- lfc_vec / se_vec
  # `multtest()` warns when locfdr falls back on its cruder estimators; the
  # estimate is still used.
  null_res <- suppressWarnings(eSVD2::multtest(z_vec[is.finite(z_vec)]))

  # The bounds of the rescaling; at least one residual direction is left.
  upper_factor <- sqrt(res$residual_df /
                         max(res$residual_df - ncol(view$x_mat), 1))
  se_factor <- min(max(null_res$null_sd, 1), upper_factor)

  data.frame(gene = colnames(view$dat),
             log2fc = lfc_vec - null_res$null_mean * stats::median(se_vec),
             se = se_factor * se_vec,
             stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
}

1.5 The score and the gates

The score of a cohort is the Gaussian negative log-likelihood of the truth under the reported pair, in nats per gene, and lower is better,

\[\text{NLL} = \frac{1}{p}\sum_{g=1}^{p}\left[\tfrac12 \log\!\left(2\pi s_g^2\right) + \frac{(\widehat\beta_g - \beta_g)^2}{2 s_g^2}\right].\]

The truth \(\beta_g\) is the marginal effect in run A and the direct effect in run B (ESVD2_TRUTH), and every block prints the score against both. A commit is kept when its paired gain over the best commit is positive and at least one paired standard error over the 288 dev examples, and when it passes two gates. slope_weak, the slope of the reported log fold change on the truth over weak-effect genes, must lie in \([0.9, 1.1]\), so that shrinkage toward zero fails. se_strong is new: the SE of strong-effect genes over the SE that genes of the same expression level without a strong effect have, pooled over the examples, must lie in \([0.92, 1.08]\), so that an SE which follows the estimate fails. The rule that the first run withdrew by hand gives se_strong 1.20 on this bank, and the valid reference rules 0.97 to 1.04.

2 The bank

The bank lfcse-bank-2 holds 288 dev and 288 test examples. An example is one cohort of 600 genes generated from the model of Section 1.1 and fitted end to end by eSVD2 1.2.0 at rank 5. Nine factors vary. Six are the first bank’s: donors (10, 20, 40), cells per donor (50 equal; unequal, 30 to 600), effects (sparse, sparse_up, dense), covariates (none; donor sex and age), donor SD (0.2, 0.5, now varying between genes), and expression in place of the rate range (high: the first bank’s gene intercepts; low: sparse genes, for which the cap on the nuisance rate binds). Three are new. state: none (\(u_d = 0\), \(s = 0\), the first bank’s case), donor (donor states carry about 72% of the donor variance), donor_arm (the same, with an arm shift \(s\)). arm_sd: the cases’ donor variance is 1.5 times and the controls’ 0.5 times the common value. depth: each donor shifts a block of 15% of the genes, which moves its total count and so every other gene’s adjusted level. Each split is a balanced 1/6 fraction of the 1728 combinations, and the two splits share no combination. BANK.md records the bank as built.

Table 1. Realized values of the bank, both splits.
Quantity Realized
Genes capped or at the boundary, expression = high 31%
Genes capped or at the boundary, expression = low 49% (first bank: 13%; real cohorts: 73%)
Mean count per cell and gene, high and low 3.15 and 0.37
Cells per cohort, 10 and 40 donors 1212 and 4728 on average

What an ideal use of the embedding could reach. oracle_state is donor_wls with each donor’s true state effect subtracted beforehand, and oracle_all subtracts the donor’s whole true effect and leaves sampling noise.

Table 2. Dev scores of donor_wls and of two oracles that read the truth, against the marginal effect.
state donor_wls oracle_state oracle_all
none 0.184 0.148 -0.748
donor 0.155 -0.210 -0.751
donor_arm 0.114 -0.222 -0.733

The donor states hold about 0.36 nats per gene at the two levels that have them. The oracle knows which part of the arms’ state difference is the population shift \(s\); no rule does, which is the point of Section 1.2.

Figure 1. Run A: the dev score of every experiment, kept commits filled.

Four experiments used the embedding to change the donor summaries or the design (2, 3, 4 and 8). Each left the log fold change where it was, because the fitted scores are orthogonal to the arm, and each made the SE too small, because the donor variation it removed from the residuals still moves the arm contrast. Experiment 5 added that variation back and reached 0.1720, and experiment 6 moved it into the prior of the moderation and reached 0.1506.

Table 4. Run A: scores against the marginal effect.
Rule Dev Test
null_rescaled 0.3066 0.2969
donor_wls 0.1508 0.1320
embed_prior 0.1506 0.1321

embed_prior gains 0.165 nats on the baseline on test (14 paired SE), all of it from leaving the posterior for a donor-level regression. Against donor_wls its difference on test is 0.0002 (paired SE 0.0014).

Against the marginal effect, no rule that uses the embedding beat donor_wls. The best one is donor_wls with a second covariate in its variance prior, and it scores the same to the fourth digit. This is what Section 1.2 predicts and not a failure of the search: the scores are orthogonal to the arm, so they cannot move the arm contrast, and the part of the contrast that lies along the loadings cannot be removed without removing a real difference between the arms.

Five commits were kept. The first removed the loadings component of the arm contrast and took the residual variance free of the embedding offset (0.297 nats). The second rescaled the SE by the empirical null’s SD (0.093), the third weighted the loadings regression and made it robust (0.011), the fourth bounded the rescaling (0.014), and the fifth added the products of the loadings (0.037), which removed the whole penalty of unequal donor variance between the arms.

state_adjusted is below both other rules in every stratum of both splits. On test it scores -0.245 at state = donor and -0.204 at donor_arm, where donor_wls scores 0.122 and 0.731. At state = none, where the embedding has no donor structure to find, it scores 0.142 against 0.181, so the adjustment costs nothing when there is nothing to adjust.

The median SE of state_adjusted is below the baseline’s where donors have states, most at donor SD 0.5, which is the donor-to-donor variation that the adjustment took out of both the estimate and its variance.

For the effect at fixed cell state, the embedding is worth 0.45 nats per gene over donor_wls on held-out cohorts (273 of 288 improved) and 0.46 over the posterior-based baseline, with a calibrated Wald statistic. The gain comes from the loadings, through a regression of the arm contrast on them across genes, and from the scores, through the residual variance.

5 Does each kept rule use the embedding?

Every fourth dev example of the bank (72 cohorts). Each rule file is sourced alone and run on the cohort’s view, on the view with the rows of the scores permuted across cells, and on the view with the rows of the loadings permuted across genes as well (diagnostics/scramble_check_claude.R).

Table 8. Each kept rule with the embedding scrambled, by state.
Rule state Median change of the logFC in SE, scores scrambled The same, scores and loadings scrambled SE ratio, scores scrambled Score (direct) Score, scores scrambled Score, both scrambled
embed_prior donor 0.013 0.015 0.996 0.203 0.201 0.208
embed_prior donor_arm 0.030 0.025 0.996 0.977 0.996 1.067
embed_prior none 0.012 0.015 0.999 0.141 0.139 0.140
state_adjusted donor 0.099 0.645 1.336 -0.132 -0.031 0.187
state_adjusted donor_arm 0.135 1.442 1.474 -0.295 -0.170 0.752
state_adjusted none 0.061 0.231 1.050 0.097 0.095 0.130

embed_prior moves by about 0.01 standard errors and scores the same when the embedding is scrambled. By the memo’s own standard (a rule whose embedding term could be deleted without changing the method), it does not use the embedding. state_adjusted uses both parts: scrambling the scores widens its SE by a factor of 1.34 to 1.47 where donors have states, and scrambling the loadings as well moves its log fold change by 0.64 to 1.44 standard errors and takes its score from -0.295 to 0.752 at donor_arm.

The price. On these cohorts state_adjusted scores 2.39 against the marginal effect at donor_arm, against 0.07 for embed_prior. It removes the arms’ difference in cell state and reports a small SE, so it is confidently wrong as an estimate of the marginal effect whenever that difference is real. On the whole test split its score against the marginal effect is 0.391.

Run A’s rule satisfies the constraint in letter only, and run B’s rule satisfies it in substance. state_adjusted and the marginal effect are incompatible by construction: the rule is right for the effect at fixed cell state and wrong for the log ratio of mean expression whenever the arms differ in cell state.

6 Constants

The truth was not on trial within either run. state_adjusted has these numeric constants, and the dev split chose the value of none of them.

Constant Where Reason
1/2 half count in \(l_{dg}\) (step 1) continuity correction of a Poisson count, which keeps the logarithm finite at a zero count
0 floor of \(\tau^2\) and \(\phi\) (step 4) a variance component is not negative
50, \(10^{-8}\) trigamma inverse in the moderation (step 4) iteration cap and single-precision tolerance of Newton’s method
3 exclusion threshold of the loadings regression, in SE (step 5) a normal residual is beyond 3 SE once in 370 genes, so a gene beyond it is taken to carry an effect of its own
2 passes of the loadings regression (step 5) one pass to find those genes, one without them; a third pass changed the score by 0.0004
1 lower bound of the SE factor (step 7) removing the offset cannot make the residual variance too large
\(\sqrt{\nu / (\nu - k)}\) upper bound of the SE factor (step 7) the offset has \(k\) free directions among the \(\nu\) residual ones and cannot have absorbed more than that share

7 Recommendation

Three statements follow from the evidence of this bank. The embedding improves the log fold change only for the effect at fixed cell state (Sections 1.2, 3 and 4). For that target state_adjusted is the best rule found, its gain holds on held-out cohorts, and its Wald statistic is calibrated (Section 4). For the marginal effect donor_wls remains the best rule known, and no use of the embedding improved it (Section 3).

The decisions below are choices the evidence does not settle, and they are Kevin’s.

  1. The target. Whether eSVD-DE’s reported log fold change is the marginal effect (the package’s current convention, and what the p-value tests) or the effect at fixed cell state. The second treats a difference in cell state between cases and controls as a nuisance, which is also a scientific claim about the disease.
  2. The memo’s decisions. Its section 6 lists nine choices Claude made without a round: the truth, the form of the state factor, rank 5, single cohorts, the expression factor, the second gate and its interval, the baseline, how the embedding constraint is checked, and the split of the design.
  3. The second run. Scoring against the direct effect was added during the session, after run A’s first experiments, and was not in the memo.
  4. Merging. Both run branches and the loop folder are local commits; nothing is merged or pushed.

For one cohort fitted by eSVD() with the fit kept, when the target is the effect at fixed cell state:

  1. Inputs. The counts, the fitted library library_mat, the design matrix, the donor and arm of each cell, and the embedding x_mat, y_mat.
  2. Check. Each arm has at least 5 donors, and \(n - q \ge 2\). The bank does not cover fewer.
  3. Fit. report_lfc_se(view) of RULE_nov11_direct_claude.R, which is state_adjusted (Section 1.4, steps 1 to 7).
  4. Output. log2fc and se per gene; the Wald statistic is log2fc / se, referred to the standard normal distribution.
  5. Report alongside. The removed vector \(\widehat d\) and the share of the variance of \(\widehat\theta_g\) over genes that the loadings regression explains, the SE factor \(f\) and whether it sits at a bound, and the log fold change of donor_wls beside it.
  6. When the target is the marginal effect instead. Use donor_wls (autoresearch_lfcse/notes/RULE_nov11_claude.R). A large explained share in step 5 then says how much of the reported contrast is a difference in cell state, with the caveat that part of it is donor sampling.

Three next experiments.

  1. The rank (a bank factor). Every cohort was fitted at rank 5 against 3 or 4 true directions. Real fits use ranks near or above the number of donors, where the scores can absorb all donor-level variation and the bound of step 7 no longer binds. A rank factor (5, 15, 30) tests whether state_adjusted survives.
  2. Effects aligned with the loadings (a bank factor). The direct effects are drawn independently of the loadings. If the disease acts through a gene program that the embedding has also learned, the loadings regression removes part of the true effect; slope_weak fell from 0.985 to 0.958 already with independent effects, because 20 regressors over 600 genes take that share of any effect.
  3. The SE factor at 40 donors (direction E4). Without the rescaling the score at 40 donors is better (experiment 10 of run B), and the empirical null’s SD is inflated there by true weak effects. A calibration that does not read the genes’ own statistics would recover it.

8 What we glossed over

  • Real cohorts. No real cohort was read. Whether the loadings of a real fit carry the arm contrast as they do here is untested, and it is the first check before the rule is used.
  • One cohort per example. The two moments of Was2CoDE’s Figure 4 need pairs of cohorts and were dropped from this bank.
  • The capped share is 49% at expression = low, still below the real cohorts’ 73%. Neither kept rule reads the nuisance rate.
  • An experiment with a units error. Experiment 4 of run A added an unweighted variance to a weighted one; it was logged as a discard and corrected in experiment 5, which was kept.
  • A scorer change after the first baseline. The switch between the two truths and the two extra score lines were added after the bank’s baseline and before any experiment; the baseline was scored again.
  • The trial function’s random seed. The fresh-context review found that it coincided with the stream that drew the true effects; it was moved in this loop’s scorer. The first loop’s scorer has the same collision and was not changed, and no rule of either loop draws random numbers.
  • Budget. The runs used 9 and 10 of 40 experiments each and were stopped by decision, for the reasons in Sections 3 and 4.
  • The package’s p-value was again not on trial.

The best commit of run B is rescored by git checkout 1cfd07b && ESVD2_TRUTH=direct Rscript autoresearch_lfcse2/harness/evaluate_claude.R dev, and that of run A by the same command at 40e7e67 without the variable. The diagnostics scripts are run from the repository root with Rscript.
